text: Scrum is the specific, named framework most teams mean when they say they're Agile — it names the roles, the meetings, and the vocabulary you'll actually hear in a standup.

A sprint is one fixed-length cycle, almost always one or two weeks. It opens with Sprint Planning, where the team picks a sprint goal; every day the team holds a short Daily Scrum to sync on progress and blockers; and it closes with a Sprint Review, demoing the finished increment, followed by a Retrospective on what to improve next sprint.

Scrum names exactly three roles. The Product Owner is the single person accountable for the backlog's priority order — they decide what gets built next. The Scrum Master facilitates ceremonies and removes blockers, rather than managing the team's work. The Developers are everyone actually building the increment — engineers, analysts, testers, whoever's hands are on the work.

Work in the backlog is written as user stories — a short description of a need from the user's point of view. A story on its own is often too vague to know when it's done, which is what acceptance criteria are for: specific, checkable conditions the finished work must satisfy before it counts as done.

Put the whole chain together: the Product Backlog holds every idea in priority order, Sprint Planning pulls a subset into the Sprint Backlog, Sprint Work runs for one to two weeks, and the sprint produces a shippable increment — not a finished feature or code that compiles, but something that could be released right now, every single sprint.
Next lesson: Kanban boards — the visual board almost every IT team actually tracks its work on, sprint or no sprint.
